protections: Confidential transport of Kubernetes API membership queries: the service-account bearer token or the client certificate and the API response must only travel over TLS (AbstractStreamProvider.openStream, TokenStreamProvider.openStream, CertificateStreamProvider).
Server authentication of the Kubernetes API peer: the configured CA file must be used and an unverifiable peer must be refused (AbstractStreamProvider.configureCaCert).

Confidentiality of replicated cluster messages in transit via EncryptInterceptor: ChannelData.getMessage() is encrypted on send and decrypted on receive, with a startup guard that keeps it upstream of TcpFailureDetector.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: Reached only when KUBERNETES_CLIENT_CERTIFICATE_FILE is set; an operator using client certificates is expected to set KUBERNETES_MASTER_PROTOCOL or OPENSHIFT_KUBE_PING_MASTER_PROTOCOL, and a non-TLS API endpoint can be deliberate (service mesh, sidecar, dev cluster). On an http URL the client certificate is not even presented, so the request is only unauthenticated and only the pod-list response is readable.

The stream provider contract is to open the URL it is given (StreamProvider.openStream); scheme choice is operator configuration and HttpsURLConnection negotiates TLS whenever the URL happens to be https, so the shared opener sees no reason to refuse http. Only the subclass knows whether it carries credentials.

Unreachable from the shipped provider: KubernetesMembershipProvider always supplies a CA path (default /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt, lines 80-82) and both StreamProvider constructors are package-private, so today only the logged warning branch exists; the class name InsecureStreamProvider advertises the unsafe choice as an explicit opt-in.

The documented promise is encryption of channel messages carrying session data (cluster-interceptor.xml lines 199-214); what stays clear is routing metadata - options, timestamp, message uniqueId, and the sender Member (host, ports, domain, payload) - and the member payload is empty unless an application sets one, so the encrypted session bytes really are covered.

Membership announcements are discovery metadata sent on a link-local multicast group from outside the interceptor chain (ChannelCoordinator starts the membership service separately, lines 156-169); they were never part of the EncryptInterceptor contract and changing the member wire format breaks mixed-version clusters.

The probe payload is the fixed TCP_FAIL_DETECT constant and the startup guard already forces EncryptInterceptor upstream of TcpFailureDetector; the direct socket write exists precisely so failure detection works without the rest of the chain, so the encrypted content of the probe carries no secret.

A message shorter than the IV is not a legitimate encrypted message, and the encrypted minimum (IV plus one padded block) is well above the IV size, so a length guard reads as a robustness nicety rather than part of the confidentiality fix; the localized key for it is orphaned, which looks like stale text from an older revision.

Both are log/debug sinks rather than the transport: the token is only interpolated when the connection fails and the header map is only printed when debug logging is on, and an in-cluster service-account token is short-lived and node-local.

masking: T1 masks T3: while the client-certificate route builds an http URL, that provider's socket factory and trust managers are never used, so the trust-all fallback cannot be exercised on that route.
T1 and T2 mask T8 on the same route: a plain-http URL that fails or is refused never reaches the debug connection log or the token-bearing IOException.

conflicts.what: Rejecting non-https URLs in the shared opener and extending what EncryptInterceptor encrypts are independent, but a blanket requirement that every provider use TLS would be a behaviour change for deployments that intentionally use a plain-HTTP API, whereas the header-encryption change needs its own wire-format decision; doing both in one patch makes it impossible to tell which change broke a cluster.

Extending encryption to the whole ChannelData package conflicts with the byte-message probes: TcpFailureDetector and TcpPingInterceptor identify their own packets by comparing msg.getMessage() with a constant before the message is decrypted downstream, and TcpFailureDetector writes its probe straight to a socket, so a whole-package cipher must be paired with a redesign of both the probe encoding and the packet filter.

Failing closed when no CA file is configured forces users onto an explicitly insecure provider, while redacting the token from logs changes the diagnostic message that users currently rely on; a single fix that both removes the fallback and refuses to log the URL must not drop the information needed to diagnose an unreachable API server.

fairness_risks: Plain-HTTP Kubernetes/OpenShift API endpoints (service mesh, sidecar, development clusters) are legitimate deployments; a blanket refusal of http in the stream provider would break them, and the scheme is currently operator-configurable.

Clusters that rely on the documented behaviour of connecting without a CA file (the abstractStream.CACertUndefined warning) and on InsecureStreamProvider would fail closed if configureCaCert stopped returning the insecure trust managers.

Encrypting the ChannelData header or the sender Member changes the wire format: a rolling upgrade from an older Tomcat would make nodes unable to parse each other's packages, and the TcpFailureDetector/TcpPingInterceptor byte-message probes depend on the current frame layout.

Encrypting multicast membership announcements would make members running an older version invisible and would require key configuration for a membership service that today has no encryption settings at all.

A minimum-length guard for decryption must not reject the legitimate shapes: a 1-byte byte-message payload (TestEncryptInterceptor.testTinyPayload) and the IV-plus-one-padded-block minimum both have to keep working.

design.why: Four independent fix sites across three layers, each with a different reason to dismiss. T1/T2 is a M5+M3 pair: an operator-controlled default that hides a whole branch (the client-certificate URL is built with http) plus the shared opener that never rejects a plaintext URL and therefore never uses the configured trust material - this is the mimo-type group (a defaulted coupled value). T3 is a M2 second trust implementation that accepts any server certificate and is unreachable today because the caller now always supplies a CA path - a deepseek-type protection-absent-with-dismissal. T4 is the M4 boundary of EncryptInterceptor: the header half of every ChannelData package, including the sender Member payload, is sent in clear while the docs promise confidentiality - xhard for deepseek. T6 is the M1 direct-socket probe in TcpFailureDetector that the startup ordering guard explicitly does not cover. The first two groups sit in the package a report would lead to; T4 and T6 force the solver into io/ and group/interceptors/, so a solver who only edits KubernetesMembershipProvider fails half the task. This beats stacking T1/T2 with T3 and T8 alone (all three collapse into the same two files of the cloud package and one guard would close the transport ones) and beats adding T5/T7 first, which are wire-format and robustness work rather than confidentiality fixes and would turn the task into a protocol redesign.

unverified: The fix commits named in the candidate (a_fix 0112ed22abfc, 607ebc0fa522, 6d955cceca84; b_fix 1fab40ccc752, 55f3eb914823, 776e12b3e2b0) are not inspectable here: the git directory is outside the permitted read root and no git command is available, so the identification of A as the https default in the token branch (KubernetesMembershipProvider.java:85-87) and B as the http default in the client-certificate branch (lines 101-103) is an inference from the code asymmetry, not a fact taken from the patches.

No advisory text is available; CWE-311 was mapped onto the only credentials handled in tomcat-tribes (the service-account token and the client key). If either advisory is instead about EncryptInterceptor coverage, T4/T5/T6 become the advisory routes and T1/T2/T3 the uncovered sites.

The A fix could equally be the caCertFile default at KubernetesMembershipProvider.java:80-82 rather than the protocol default; in that reading T3 is the already-fixed A route and only T1/T2 remain as the incompletely fixed area.

T7 is a robustness/DoS gap (an uncaught runtime exception for a message shorter than the IV) and T8 is CWE-532 credential logging, not a CWE-311 confidentiality fix; whether either is in scope for this candidate is unknown.
No test in the tree exercises the cloud StreamProviders (only TestKubernetesJson exists), so the reachability statements for T1/T2/T3 rest on the env-var code paths, not on an exercised test.
